original_description.summary: From Earth’s assembly out of the early Solar System to a biologically transformed planet with plate tectonics, oceans, atmospheric oxygen, forests, and complex ecosystems.
original_description.climate: Hadean heat gave way to liquid-water oceans, fluctuating greenhouse climates, global glaciations, and today’s interglacial.
original_description.geo: Earth differentiated into a core, mantle and crust. Tectonics assembled and dispersed supercontinents repeatedly.
original_description.continents: Continental crust developed over billions of years. Ocean basins have repeatedly opened and closed.
original_description.life: Life was microbial for most of Earth’s history; multicellular organisms and land ecosystems diversified relatively recently.
original_description.etym: Earth: from Old English eorþe, “ground, soil, world.”
events: ≥3.5 Ga: strong evidence of microbial life
~2.4 Ga: major rise in atmospheric oxygen

original_description.summary: Earth forms from the solar nebula. Core segregation, impacts and early crust formation establish the conditions for oceans.
original_description.climate: Initially extremely hot, later cooler enough for solid crust and likely surface water in portions of the eon.
original_description.geo: Giant impacts, magma oceans, core formation, oldest surviving zircons (~4.4 Ga).
original_description.continents: No stable modern-style continents; early crust was repeatedly reworked.
original_description.life: No confirmed life from the Hadean.
original_description.etym: Named for Hades, Greek realm of the dead, evoking an early high-energy Earth.
events: ~4.4 Ga: ancient zircons imply low-temperature interaction with water

original_description.summary: Earth’s earliest large-scale biological record: microbial mats, oxygenic photosynthesis and growing continental nuclei.
original_description.climate: Oceans persist under a Sun fainter than today; greenhouse gases probably helped maintain liquid water.
original_description.geo: Cratons and granite-greenstone terranes develop, and banded iron formations accumulate.
original_description.continents: Small continental nuclei and greenstone belts, with tectonic regimes still debated.
original_description.life: Bacteria and archaea thrive; photosynthetic microbial ecosystems expand.
original_description.etym: Greek arkhaîos, “ancient, original.”
events: Early oxygenic photosynthesis before atmospheric oxygenation

original_description.summary: Oxygen reshapes the atmosphere and oceans, eukaryotes evolve, supercontinents cycle and early animals emerge.
original_description.climate: Great Oxidation Event, later long-lasting oxygen changes and Neoproterozoic snowball-earth glaciations.
original_description.geo: Banded iron formations, extensive sedimentary successions, continental collisions and major glaciations.
original_description.continents: Columbia/Nuna, Rodinia and associated supercontinental cycles; Gondwana later assembles.
original_description.life: Eukaryotes, algae and multicellularity become established; Ediacaran organisms appear late.
original_description.etym: Greek próteros “earlier” + zōḗ “life”; life predating conspicuous Phanerozoic fossils.

original_description.summary: A vast diversification of complex life, the colonization of land, forests, dinosaurs, birds, mammals and humans.
original_description.climate: Alternation between greenhouse and icehouse worlds, punctuated by abrupt changes and major extinction crises.
original_description.geo: Extensive fossil-bearing strata, mountain belts, ocean-basin opening and closing and major volcanic provinces.
original_description.continents: Pangaea assembled and broke apart; the Atlantic opened and present continents drifted toward modern positions.
original_description.life: Cambrian animal diversification, land plants and vertebrates, Mesozoic ecosystems and Cenozoic radiations.
original_description.etym: Greek phanerós “visible” + zōḗ “life”; conspicuous animal fossils.

original_description.summary: The earliest surviving crustal rocks and mineral evidence of an ancient hydrosphere.
original_description.geo: Acasta gneiss and other ancient terrains constrain early continental-crust development.

original_description.summary: Ancient microbial communities develop within early ocean ecosystems.
original_description.life: Stromatolite and microbial biosignatures become increasingly abundant.

original_description.summary: Growing continental crust, marine microbial ecosystems and increasingly complex geochemical cycles.
Oxygenic photosynthesis becomes important before oxygen accumulates substantially in the atmosphere.
The atmosphere oxygenates, life responds, and large continental masses grow.
events: ~2.1 Ga: early large multicellular fossils (interpretation debated)

original_description.summary: Stable large continental interiors, Rodinia assembly and diversification of eukaryotic algae.
Rodinia breaks up; dramatic glaciations precede the rise of conspicuous multicellular life.
An interval of extensive iron deposition and the beginning of sustained atmospheric oxygen accumulation.
original_description.etym: Greek sídēros “iron”; widespread iron-rich sediments.

original_description.summary: Early Paleoproterozoic climate disruptions and glacial deposits linked to changing atmospheric chemistry.
original_description.etym: Greek rhýax “stream of lava,” referring to widespread volcanism.

original_description.summary: Continental collisions and early large-scale supercontinental assembly.
original_description.etym: Greek óros “mountain,” alluding to major orogenic events.

original_description.summary: Relative stabilization and growth of many continental blocks.
original_description.etym: Greek statherós “stable,” referring to relatively stable cratons.

original_description.summary: Platform sedimentation covers old continental cores.
original_description.etym: Greek kálymma “cover,” referring to widespread sedimentary cover.

original_description.summary: Rift basins and eukaryotic algae occur across continental margins.
original_description.etym: Greek éktasis “extension”; extension of sedimentary covers.

original_description.summary: Rodinia assembly and widespread Grenvillian mountain-building.
original_description.etym: Greek stenós “narrow,” referring to narrow metamorphic belts.

original_description.summary: Rodinia begins to fragment; complex eukaryotes and early animal-lineage evolution are investigated.
original_description.etym: Greek tónos “stretch,” referring to continental stretching.

original_description.summary: Prolonged Sturtian and Marinoan ice ages may have extended ice toward low latitudes.
original_description.climate: Two major glacial episodes bracket extensive ocean and atmosphere changes; “Snowball Earth” extent remains debated.
original_description.geo: Glacial deposits occur on multiple former continents, often capped by distinctive carbonates.
original_description.life: Marine microorganisms and eukaryotes persisted in environmental refugia.
original_description.etym: Greek krýos “cold, frost” + -genian “producing.”

original_description.summary: Large-bodied soft organisms diversify before the Cambrian; some may represent early animals, others extinct experimental body plans.
original_description.climate: Following Marinoan deglaciation, variable ocean oxygen and nutrient conditions.
original_description.geo: Ediacaran fossil assemblages preserve soft-body impressions in sandstones.
original_description.continents: Gondwana assembles; shallow seas spread around continental margins.
original_description.life: Dickinsonia, rangeomorphs and other Ediacaran biota; early burrowing and biomineralizing animals toward the end.
original_description.etym: Named for Australia’s Ediacara Hills, renowned for enigmatic late Precambrian fossils.
events: ~575 Ma: diversification of Ediacaran macroscopic fossils

original_description.summary: Marine animal diversity expands; plants and animals colonize land and vast forests develop. Ends with Earth’s largest known mass extinction.
original_description.climate: Early warm seas; late Paleozoic glaciation and changing atmospheric oxygen/CO₂.
original_description.geo: Appalachian and Variscan orogenies, widespread limestones, giant coal swamps.
original_description.continents: Gondwana spans the south while Laurentia, Baltica and others converge into Pangaea.
original_description.life: Trilobites, fishes, land plants, insects, amphibians and amniotes diversify.
original_description.etym: Greek palaiós “ancient” + zōḗ “life.”

original_description.summary: Dinosaurs, pterosaurs and marine reptiles proliferate while early mammals and birds evolve; flowering plants diversify near its end.
original_description.climate: Predominantly greenhouse conditions with relatively warm poles and generally high Mesozoic sea levels.
original_description.geo: Central Atlantic Magmatic Province at the Triassic–Jurassic boundary and major Cretaceous oceanic events.
original_description.continents: Pangaea fragments into Laurasia and Gondwana; early Atlantic opens.
original_description.life: Dinosaur-dominated terrestrial faunas, gymnosperms, marine reptiles, ammonites and emerging angiosperms.
original_description.etym: Greek mésos “middle” + zōḗ “life.”

original_description.summary: Modern mammal and bird lineages radiate; grasslands spread, global climate cools and hominins eventually appear.
original_description.climate: Paleogene warmth gives way to Antarctic glaciation and later Northern Hemisphere ice sheets.
original_description.geo: Himalayan uplift, Antarctic ice sheets, global cooling and Quaternary glacial cycles.
original_description.continents: India collides with Asia; Australia separates from Antarctica; Atlantic widens.
original_description.life: Mammals, birds, flowering plants, grasses, primates and hominins diversify.
original_description.etym: Greek kainós “new, recent” + zōḗ “life.”

original_description.summary: Rapid diversification and preservation of many major animal body plans and ecological interactions in the sea.
original_description.climate: Generally warm marine conditions, with changing sea levels and oxygenation.
original_description.geo: Transgressive shallow seas and excellent fossil deposits including the Burgess Shale (~508 Ma).
original_description.continents: Gondwana mostly in the Southern Hemisphere, with Laurentia, Baltica and Siberia separated by oceans.
original_description.life: Arthropods, early chordates, molluscs, sponges, echinoderms and predators diversify.
original_description.etym: Latin Cambria, the Romanized name for Wales, where Cambrian rocks were studied.

original_description.summary: The Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event transforms marine communities.
original_description.climate: Initially greenhouse-like, with major glaciation near the end.
original_description.geo: Thick carbonates, widespread reefs and Taconic orogeny.
original_description.continents: Gondwana migrates across high southern latitudes; epicontinental seas cover continents.
original_description.life: Brachiopods, bryozoans, crinoids, cephalopods and jawless fishes diversify; early land plants may appear.
original_description.etym: Named for the Ordovices, an ancient Welsh Celtic people.

original_description.summary: Life rebounds after Ordovician extinctions and vascular plants expand onto land.
original_description.climate: Recovery from late Ordovician glaciation; warm shallow seas spread.
original_description.geo: Caledonian mountain-building, extensive reef carbonates and evaporites.
original_description.continents: Laurentia and Baltica collide as the Iapetus Ocean closes.
original_description.life: Jawed fishes diversify; land arthropods and small vascular plants become more conspicuous.
original_description.etym: Named for the Silures, a Celtic people of ancient Wales.

original_description.summary: The “Age of Fishes”: vascular plants form the first large forests while lobe-finned vertebrates approach terrestrial life.
original_description.climate: Early warmth shifts toward cooling; ocean anoxia accompanies later extinction pulses.
original_description.geo: Old Red Sandstone deposits, reef complexes, Acadian orogeny and widespread organic-rich black shales.
original_description.continents: Euramerica forms; Gondwana remains large in the south.
original_description.life: Placoderms, sharks, lobe-finned fishes, seed plants, trees and early tetrapods diversify.
original_description.etym: Named for Devon, England, where its strata were studied.

original_description.summary: Humid equatorial forests create extensive coal deposits; tetrapods and amniotes diversify.
original_description.climate: Late Paleozoic icehouse with Gondwanan glaciations and humid tropical coal swamps.
original_description.geo: Coal measures, cyclic marine transgressions and Appalachian–Variscan orogenies.
original_description.continents: Pangaea assembles as Gondwana collides with Euramerica.
original_description.life: Giant lycopsids, horsetails, ferns, large insects, amphibians and early amniotes flourish.
original_description.etym: Latin carbo “coal” + ferre “to bear”: coal-bearing sediments.

original_description.summary: Pangaea’s vast continental interior becomes strongly seasonal and arid; synapsids diversify before catastrophic extinction.
original_description.climate: Late Paleozoic ice wanes; hot, arid continental interiors expand.
original_description.geo: Red beds, evaporites, extensive volcanism and Siberian Traps eruptions near the end.
original_description.continents: Pangaea dominates, flanked by Panthalassa and the Tethys Ocean.
original_description.life: Pelycosaur-grade and therapsid synapsids, conifers and seed plants prosper; trilobites disappear at its close.
original_description.etym: Named for Perm, Russia, where characteristic rocks were described.

original_description.summary: Ecosystems recover from the end-Permian crisis; first dinosaurs, pterosaurs and mammals emerge.
original_description.climate: Hot and often strongly seasonal, especially on Pangaea’s immense interior.
original_description.geo: Rift basins and later Central Atlantic Magmatic Province flood basalts.
original_description.continents: Pangaea is still joined but begins to rift; large Tethyan coasts.
original_description.life: Early archosaurs, dinosaurs, pterosaurs, mammaliaforms and marine reptile groups arise; ammonoids recover.
original_description.etym: From German Trias “triad,” for a threefold succession of strata recognized in Germany.

original_description.summary: Large sauropods and other dinosaurs dominate many land faunas; birds originate within theropod dinosaurs.
original_description.climate: Mostly warm greenhouse conditions with limited evidence of extensive continental ice.
original_description.geo: Shallow continental shelves, marine limestones and expanding Atlantic rifts.
original_description.continents: North Atlantic begins opening as Pangaea divides into Laurasia and Gondwana.
original_description.life: Sauropods, stegosaurs, theropods, pterosaurs, ammonites and early birds diversify.
original_description.etym: Named for the Jura Mountains between France and Switzerland.
events: ~150 Ma: Archaeopteryx and early bird evolution

original_description.summary: Flowering plants transform terrestrial ecosystems, dinosaur diversity remains high and the era ends with a major impact-linked extinction.
original_description.climate: Generally warm greenhouse, very high sea levels and intervals of widespread oceanic anoxia.
original_description.geo: Chalk and limestone deposition, mid-ocean ridge activity, Deccan Traps eruptions and Chicxulub impact.
original_description.continents: Continents separate further; Western Interior Seaway splits North America; India moves north.
original_description.life: Angiosperms and associated insects radiate; birds, mammals and teleost fishes diversify alongside non-avian dinosaurs.
original_description.etym: Latin creta “chalk,” for widespread chalk deposits formed largely from microscopic marine plankton.
events: 66 Ma: Chicxulub impact and K–Pg extinction

original_description.summary: Mammals and birds radiate after the K–Pg extinction; the world changes from very warm to increasingly cool.
original_description.climate: Paleocene–Eocene warming culminating in a thermal maximum; Antarctic ice sheets expand near 34 Ma.
original_description.geo: Himalayan–Alpine mountain-building and onset of major Antarctic glaciation.
original_description.continents: India continues northward; Atlantic widens; Southern Ocean gateways evolve.
original_description.life: Primates, ungulates, carnivoran precursors, cetaceans and modern bird groups proliferate.
original_description.etym: Greek palaiós “ancient” + -genḗs “born”; older part of the Cenozoic.

original_description.summary: Grasslands and grazers diversify, ape lineages radiate and hominins emerge in Africa.
original_description.climate: Long-term cooling and drying punctuated by warm Miocene intervals.
original_description.geo: Widespread marine sediments, basin formation, uplift and reorganized ocean circulation.
original_description.continents: Himalayas rise further, East African rifting develops and Panama isthmus approaches closure.
original_description.life: Grasses, grazing mammals, great apes, hominins and many modern genera diversify.
original_description.etym: Greek néos “new” + -genḗs “born”; younger part of the Cenozoic.

original_description.summary: Repeated ice-age cycles reshape habitats while humans evolve and ultimately spread across the planet.
original_description.climate: Glacial–interglacial cycles, then the comparatively warm Holocene interglacial.
original_description.geo: Glacial till, loess, moraines, lowered ice-age sea levels and young volcanic terrains.
original_description.continents: Near-modern arrangement; ice sheets alter shorelines and expose continental shelves.
original_description.life: Mammoths and other megafauna, modern humans and extensive late Quaternary extinctions.
original_description.etym: Latin quartus “fourth”; historical fourth division of younger stratigraphic deposits.

original_description.summary: An end-Ordovician glaciation and extinction event strongly affect marine life.
Early limbed vertebrates coexist with enormous reef systems before biotic crises.
Extensive shallow seas and diversified crinoids, with land forests advancing.
Coal forests, early amniotes and diverse large arthropods populate equatorial wetlands.
Ecological recovery after the devastating end-Permian extinction.
Dinosaurs and early mammaliaforms evolve as Pangaea starts to break apart.
A famous interval for large sauropod faunas and Archaeopteryx.
Flowering plants first become conspicuous in the fossil record; many major dinosaur and bird lineages persist.
Flowering plants radiate extensively; near the end, Chicxulub impact accompanies the K–Pg extinction.
Early Cenozoic recovery and diversification after the end-Cretaceous extinction.
original_description.life: Mammalian and avian groups spread into ecological roles vacated by non-avian dinosaurs.
original_description.etym: Greek palaiós “old” + kainós “recent.”

original_description.summary: Extremely warm early Eocene conditions precede progressive cooling.
original_description.climate: Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum occurs just before the Eocene; Early Eocene Climatic Optimum follows.
original_description.life: Early whales, horses, primates and many forest-associated mammals diversify.
original_description.etym: Greek ēṓs “dawn” + kainós “recent”: dawn of many modern mammalian lineages.
events: ~56 Ma: rapid carbon injection and warming at PETM boundary

original_description.summary: Antarctic ice sheets and cooler climates restructure ecosystems.
original_description.climate: Sharp cooling and Antarctic ice-sheet expansion near the epoch start.
original_description.life: Open habitats become more widespread; mammalian faunas turn over.
original_description.etym: Greek olígos “few” + kainós “recent,” reflecting relatively few modern molluscan forms recognized in original classification.

original_description.summary: Apes radiate, grassy ecosystems expand and modern oceanic currents develop.
original_description.climate: Middle Miocene warmth followed by cooling and increased aridity.
original_description.life: Ape diversity, grasses, grazing herbivores and marine mammals diversify.
original_description.etym: Greek meíōn “less” + kainós “recent,” based on proportions of living molluscan forms.

original_description.summary: Cooling intensifies as ecosystems approach the ice-age world.
original_description.climate: A generally warmer early Pliocene transitions toward Northern Hemisphere glaciation.
original_description.life: Early hominins and increasingly modern mammal communities.
original_description.etym: Greek pleíōn “more” + kainós “recent,” reflecting the larger fraction of modern molluscs.

original_description.summary: Repeated glacial cycles and a remarkable megafauna accompany hominin expansion.
original_description.climate: Ice sheets wax and wane in repeated orbital-paced cycles.
original_description.life: Mammoths, saber-toothed cats, archaic humans and eventually Homo sapiens.
original_description.etym: Greek pleîstos “most” + kainós “recent,” indicating a very high proportion of modern molluscan species.

original_description.summary: The current interglacial: agriculture, cities and large human environmental impacts.
original_description.climate: Relatively stable postglacial warmth compared with glacial–interglacial swings; recent anthropogenic warming.
original_description.life: Modern ecosystems under growing human influence.
original_description.etym: Greek hólos “whole, entire” + kainós “recent,” meaning entirely recent.
events: ~12–10 ka: agriculture arises in several regions

original_description.summary: Directly after the K–Pg mass extinction, mammal, bird and marine food webs reorganize.
events: Post-impact ecological recovery and new mammal radiations

original_description.summary: Early Eocene greenhouse climates promote tropical and subtropical forests at high latitudes.
original_description.climate: Some of the warmest sustained Cenozoic climates.

original_description.summary: Early whales transition into more fully aquatic forms; warm forests persist.
After Eocene–Oligocene cooling, major ice expands on Antarctica.
original_description.climate: The Antarctic icehouse becomes established.

original_description.summary: The Mediterranean undergoes the Messinian Salinity Crisis, producing thick evaporite deposits.
original_description.geo: Widespread Mediterranean evaporites from extreme basin restriction (~5.97–5.33 Ma).

original_description.summary: Rapid refilling of the Mediterranean at the beginning of the Pliocene is a leading explanation for its re-connection to the Atlantic.
Quaternary glaciations intensify; large ice-age climate oscillations reshape habitats.
Middle Pleistocene glacial cycles and changing hominin communities.
Anatomically modern humans spread globally; large mammals decline in many regions.
Early Holocene warming follows the end of the Younger Dryas cold episode.
Mid-Holocene civilizations and landscape changes unfold under relatively warm conditions.
Late Holocene histories of agriculture, states, urbanization and industrialization.
Diversifying flowering plants become clearer in terrestrial fossil assemblages.
Warm seas and widespread marine ecosystems accompany elevated atmospheric CO₂.
The last age of non-avian dinosaurs and ammonites ends at the 66 Ma K–Pg extinction.
events: 66 Ma: Chicxulub impact; non-avian dinosaurs and ammonites become extinct

original_description.summary: Early bird relatives and large theropod and sauropod faunas inhabit Late Jurassic ecosystems.
The Carnian Pluvial Episode involves notable environmental disruptions; dinosaur diversification occurs across the Triassic.
Massive environmental disruption culminates in the end-Permian extinction.
Kellwasser-related environmental disruptions contribute to Late Devonian marine extinctions.
Trace fossils signal increasing animal movement and sediment mixing in early Cambrian seas.
Diverse Cambrian marine communities include spectacular soft-bodied fossil deposits.
Rapid glaciation and sea-level change coincide with the end-Ordovician extinction.

note: Primary chronology from Deep Time Atlas; alternate Tree of Life boundaries retained under source_assertions.
